claims.text: The target material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy in nanoscale thin-film or patterned-nanoribbon form.
The as-deposited films intrinsically have high film/substrate interfacial thermal resistance.
A nanoscale interlayer or engineered substrate interface can enhance thermal coupling and reduce interfacial thermal resistance.
Heat-transfer limitations dominate the proposed low-field cooling cycles near room temperature.
Reducing film/substrate thermal resistance will minimize interfacial temperature gradients and localized thermal nonuniformities.
Interfacial temperature gradients and localized nonuniformities disrupt a cooperative magnetostructural transformation in the as-deposited alloy.
Enhanced thermal coupling will promote a more cooperative magnetostructural phase transition.
A more spatially uniform transition will reduce kinetic barriers.
A more spatially uniform transition will reduce hysteretic losses during cooling cycles.
The engineered interface will decrease magnetic hysteresis-loop area relative to the unmodified as-deposited control.
The engineered interface will produce a sharper magnetocaloric transition relative to the unmodified control.
The engineered interface will produce a more reversible magnetocaloric response relative to the unmodified control.
The baseline films have less-cooperative magnetostructural transitions and larger hysteresis because of their high interfacial thermal resistance.
The baseline films have reduced magnetocaloric performance because their magnetostructural transitions are disrupted.
Magnetocaloric response shape and hysteretic losses are relevant to refrigeration performance.
Nanoscale material can have a lower maximum magnetic entropy change than a corresponding bulk material while retaining comparable relative cooling power through a broader effective temperature range.
The proposed effect is limited to low-field, near-room-temperature operation in nanoscale films and may not extend to high fields, bulk materials, or systems with negligible interfacial effects.
Nanoscale defects or compositional variations may also affect phase-transition dynamics.
